title: Lawmakers Say Anti-India Hate Is Turning Violent After Illinois Temple Plot
excerpt: Schumer, Cornyn, Rosen and Krishnamoorthi lead a bipartisan condemnation of the alleged Aurora temple plot, as a caucus cites a 240% surge in anti-South Asian hate speech and advocates seek FBI scrutiny of online extremism.
body:
• US lawmakers from both parties have condemned the alleged plot against Sri Venkateswara Temple in Aurora, Illinois, saying anti-Indian and anti-Hindu rhetoric is turning into violence — the new development is the scale and seniority of that response.
  • Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, Senators John Cornyn and Jacky Rosen, and Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi were among those who praised police for foiling the plot and called for action against white supremacist extremism.
  • The Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus said anti-South Asian hate speech on X has surged 240% in two years, linking online rhetoric to the threat against a house of worship.
  • Advocacy groups urged the FBI and Justice Department to scrutinize online influencers promoting anti-Indian extremism, and urged community members to report threats.

The political response to the alleged plot against a Hindu temple in Illinois widened sharply this week, as senior US lawmakers argued that anti-Indian hatred is no longer only online rhetoric. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said that rhetoric is at an alarming level and is now turning into violence, according to The Hindu BusinessLine reporting of his post on X.

Schumer added that bigotry against any community has no place in America and that everyone should be able to practice their faith openly. Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas and Democratic Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada also praised timely police action. Rosen said the plot had shaken the Hindu community across the country and that targeting any religious community is unacceptable.

"Anti-Indian and anti-Hindu rhetoric is at an alarming level in America."

— Senator Chuck Schumer

Krishnamoorthi and the caucus response

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, the Indian American congressman from Illinois, gave the most direct community framing. In reporting carried by Devdiscourse (ANI), he said he was horrified that a white supremacist allegedly attempted to massacre Indian Americans at the Aurora temple, thanked coworkers who sounded the alarm and officers who intervened, and said every American deserves to worship without fear.

https://x.com/NewsMatrixIND/status/2110582637261910494

The Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus, in a statement signed by lawmakers including Suhas Subramanyam, Grace Meng and Judy Chu, said the plot exposes the danger white supremacist ideology poses to communities and houses of worship and cannot be viewed in isolation. The caucus said anti-South Asian hate speech on X alone has surged 240% over the past two years, driven in part by influential figures amplifying racist rhetoric.

Other lawmakers echoed the call for leaders to lower the temperature. Rep. Tom Suozzi said leaders who vilify people for race, religion or background tear at the nation's fabric. Rep. Greg Stanton called the alleged plot an act of white supremacist hate against Indian Americans. Rep. Jonathan Jackson of Illinois called on President Donald Trump to condemn the violence by name. The ADL and the Pakistani-American Public Affairs Committee also expressed concern, with the latter noting Krishnamoorthi and his family were at the temple, according to BusinessLine.

What happened — briefly

As The Videshi reported on October 15, a 19-year-old from Palatine, identified in ANI reporting as Alexandros Paporakis, was arrested in connection with an alleged plan to attack Sri Venkateswara Temple in Aurora. He appeared in court on October 14 and was charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of weapons, and was ordered detained. Investigators said they recovered a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds, tactical equipment and body armor, and a document expressing white supremacist ideology and hostility toward people of Indian descent. BusinessLine reported the attempted attack on Sunday failed when a gun jammed; ANI reporting said detectives believed an attack had been planned for October 11.

What advocates are asking for now

The Indian American Advocacy Council urged the FBI and the Justice Department to intensify scrutiny of online hate influencers who promote anti-Indian extremism, warning that online hatred has escalated into real-world terrorism. The Hindu American Foundation urged community members to remain vigilant and report potential threats, noting the plot came during Navaratri gatherings and two weeks after an attack on a Hindu temple in Ohio, according to ANI reporting.

India's Consulate General in Chicago said it appreciated law enforcement's timely action, was in touch with diaspora members, and was monitoring developments. For temple communities, the takeaway is practical: report threats to local police and the FBI promptly during festival season.

What happens next

The suspect remains detained on the state charges as the case proceeds. The political question is whether the bipartisan condemnation produces concrete steps — federal scrutiny of online extremist networks, added protection for houses of worship, or both. Lawmakers have now placed the temple plot in a national pattern of rising anti-South Asian hate, not as an isolated local incident, and that framing will shape how agencies respond.
